How can it also be said that the name "prajñā" applies up to the sixth bhūmi, while from the seventh bhūmi onward, as prajñā becomes pure, it is instead called "upāya"?
The answer is as explained previously:
at the time of the sixth stage,
the essence of *prajñā* is strong while the function of skillful means (*upāya*) is weak.
It is subtle because its essence is firm;
it is because, through tranquil contemplation,
one contemplates emptiness without attachment.
Because their faculties are weak,
they are unable to immediately enter emptiness while traversing existence; they remain obstructed by the duality of existence and non-existence until they reach the seventh stage.
Thus, essence and function are both equal.
Being able to contemplate emptiness without being stained,
one is simultaneously able to engage with existence without attachment.
Therefore, it is called the Stage of Equal Concentration and Wisdom.
The Stage of Equal Concentration and Wisdom is precisely the skillful application of *prajñā*.
Therefore, it is said that they "reverse.
That is to say, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, both types of wisdom are skillful;
if one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, [they become even more so].
Thus, the two types of wisdom are identical in their reversal;
the wisdom of reality, being reversed, is named *sarbajñā* (all-knowledge),
which refers to omniscience (*sarvajña*).
The reversal of skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) is termed the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Question: If these two are termed the "two knowledges" upon reaching the fruit, then in the causal stage they must likewise be identical to the "two wisdoms."
Why was it previously stated that while *prajñā* is called "wisdom" (*hui*), skillful means (*upāya*) is not so named?
The answer is: names established according to cause and effect each have their own specific significance.
Within the category of the fruit, that which illuminates the objective realm of all emptiness is termed "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*).
That which illuminates all objects of existence is called "omniscience" (sarvākārajñatā).
Since both [terms] are established by way of their objects,
it is appropriate to refer to them both as "knowledge" (jñāna).

Because the wisdom of the causal gate (*hetu-mukha*) is designated as "wisdom" based on its function in relation to its objects and skillful means, it cannot be called "wisdom" in the same sense [as the path].
Question: If that is so, why are both the bodhisattva’s *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths) and *mārgākārajñatā* (knowledge of the aspects of the paths) both termed "wisdom"?
Answer: Within the wisdom pertaining to the causal stage, there are naturally many categories, each established with a different name:
the wisdom of the path (mārgajñatā) and the wisdom of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā).
These names are also established based on their respective objects;
therefore, they should both be designated as "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

Question: If that is so, one should simply speak of "path-wisdom" (*mārga-prajñā*) and "knowledge of the aspects of the path" (*mārgākāra-jñatā*); yet upon reaching the fruition, why are they instead named "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) and "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
Question: Why is it said that *prajñā* and skillful means (*upāya*) are instead termed the two wisdoms?
Answer: The treatise states that within the causal stage, they are termed *prajñā*.
Since "all-knowledge" (sarvajñā) is the name for the fruit,
by the logical principle of the means within the cause, it is correspondingly named "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā).
These two wisdoms are correspondingly termed the two knowledges.
Therefore, it does not depend on words.
The *Wenlun* (Treatise on Questions) states:
"Prajñā is, conversely, sarvajñā."
Question: Why is it that what is called "expedient means" (upāya) is, conversely, named "all-aspect wisdom" (sarvākārajñatā)?
Answer: Prajñā is named "wisdom" (prajñā);
it is a term for the illumination of objects.
The omniscience of the stage of fruition is likewise designated according to its illumination of objects,
because these two names correspond to their respective primary characteristics.
It is said that the cause is named *prajñā* (wisdom) and the fruit is named "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*).
"Skillful means" (*upāya*) is designated by its functional application, while "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is so named because it encompasses all aspects.
The names are established based on their respective objects;
since these two meanings differ,
the sūtras and śāstras do not state that the skillful means themselves constitute the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience).
Although the name "expedient means" (upāya) is not established based on its object,
its essence actually illuminates existence; therefore,
it conversely becomes the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Although there is no explicit textual passage [to this effect],
the underlying principle and logic must be so.
Furthermore, within the causal stage, these are termed the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real.
The fruit is termed the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real;
this may also be taken as the text itself.
This concludes the fourth section, the Gate of Objects and Wisdom, in the Treatise.
Wisdom does not arise in isolation;
it must necessarily be triggered by an object.
Therefore, the object is the foundation of wisdom.
Objects do not exist independently;
they receive their designation through cognition.
Therefore, cognition is the fundamental basis of objects.
Therefore, there can be no arising of wisdom without an object;
there can be no illumination of an object without wisdom.
Since there can be no arising of wisdom without an object, [the two are mutually dependent].
The objective realm is that which gives rise [to cognition],
and wisdom is that which is given rise to;
for without wisdom, there would be no means to illumine the objective realm.
Wisdom is that which illuminates, while the object is that which is illuminated.
The object is that which gives rise [to wisdom] and is what is illuminated by wisdom;
thus, the object acts as the basis for wisdom.
If wisdom is that which illuminates and is produced by the object,
then wisdom would be the object;
for it is the object that is illuminated which produces the wisdom.
The object is the capacity for which cognition acts;
because cognition, being brought forth by that [object], is able to illuminate the object.
The object is the capacity for which cognition acts.
One must not say that the object is prior and the cognition is posterior;
nor that the cognition is prior and the object is posterior;
nor that they are simultaneous.
It can only be termed the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya) of cognition.
Question: By taking what as its object is cognition produced?
Answer: Because the Tathāgata always teaches the Dharma by relying upon the two truths.
The two truths are called "teachings" because they can give rise to the two types of wisdom;
the two truths are called "objects" because they are the spheres of that wisdom.
The Dharma Master Tanyi of Guanzhong annotated the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*,
receiving the oral instructions of Master Kumārajīva directly.
Master Kumārajīva said:
"The transmission of my teachings rests upon Dao Rong, Tan Ying, and Seng Rui.
Master Ying’s preface on the Two Truths states:
According to ultimate truth, there is no existence;
according to conventional truth, there is no non-existence.
Because it is ultimate, there is no existence.
Though non-existent, it exists;
because it is conventional, it is not non-existent.
Though existent, it does not exist.
Though non-existent, it exists;
yet it does not stagnate in non-existence.
Though existent, it is non-existent.
Because one is not burdened by existence and does not stagnate in non-existence,
one cuts off the view of annihilation.
Because it is not burdened by existence,
it is like ice constantly melting away.
Because it is tranquil regarding these extremes, it is called the Middle.
To examine this meaning in detail:
because it is real, it does not exist;
yet although it does not exist, it exists.
This is precisely the unmoving true limit (bhūtakoṭi),
yet it establishes all phenomena; because they are conventional,
there is neither existence nor non-existence.
Though they exist, they are non-existent;

this is precisely to explain the true nature (dharmatā) without destroying conventional designations (prajñapti). By explaining the true nature without destroying conventional designations, although they are called "conventional designations," [they are in fact empty].
It is the very likeness of the true mark;
unmoving from the limit of reality,
it establishes all dharmas.
Although it is called the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
it is nonetheless all phenomena;
because the limit of reality is nonetheless all phenomena.
Not stagnating in non-existence,
the true mark of all phenomena remains vividly present;
thus, one is not burdened by existence.
Because it is not burdened by existence, it is not eternal;
because it does not stagnate in non-existence, it is not annihilated.
This is precisely the Middle Way.
From these two truths, two types of wisdom arise;
because they realize the true nature of all phenomena,
they give rise to *upāya-prajñā* (skillful means and wisdom).
Because of awakening to the true mark of all dharmas,
there arises prajñā-upāya;
through upāya-prajñā, it is perfectly manifest as upāya.
Because *upāya* is perfectly integrated with *prajñā*, it is truly *prajñā*.
Because *upāya* is perfectly integrated with *prajñā*,
one does not cling to existence.
Because Prajñā is perfectly integrated with Upāya, it does not stagnate in non-existence;
because it is not encumbered by existence, it is eternally like ice melting away.
Because it does not stagnate in non-existence, it severs the view of nihilism and brings it to cessation.
Because it is quiescent regarding these extremes, it is called the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).
Thus, through the middle way of the two truths,
the middle way of the two wisdoms is further generated.
The contemplation within the two wisdoms further illuminates the middle way of the two truths; thus,
the object accords with the wisdom.
When cognition accords with its object,
that object is called the "object of cognition," and that cognition is called "cognition of the object."
Since the two objects have now been correctly elucidated and the meaning of the two wisdoms is clear,
it is necessary to distinguish the wisdoms by means of their respective objects.
That those of the two vehicles do not attain the two kinds of knowledge is precisely because they do not perceive these two truths;
they fail to attain correct contemplation.
This is also because one does not perceive that the two truths are themselves the Middle Way.

Question: If Prajñā illuminates the true mark of all dharmas and Upāya illuminates all dharmas as the true mark, then it follows that Prajñā does not illuminate all dharmas and Upāya does not illuminate the true mark.
Is it not that [the Bodhisattva] has not restricted the Sage’s mind, thereby losing its unimpeded, wondrous function?
Answer: Prajñā is the essence of upāya, and upāya is the function of prajñā.
The essence reflects the true mark,
while its function illuminates all phenomena;
therefore, these two gates are opened.
Thus, wisdom is perfectly complete without exception,
and its illumination is exhaustive without remainder.
If one illuminates the true reality (bhūtatathatā) in this same way, [it is so].
Simultaneously reflecting upon all phenomena,
these two objects are not differentiated,
and the two wisdoms mutually reflect one another.
Question: If the old explanation is also like this, how does it differ from the present one?
Answer: The essence of *prajñā* is not incapable of illuminating all phenomena;
however, since its function already illuminates them, there is no need for *prajñā* itself to illuminate them further.
If the function already illuminates all phenomena,
yet its essence also illuminates them,
then there would be two illuminations directed toward a single object.
It would also follow that a single cognition could arise with respect to two objects;
therefore, two types of wisdom do not illuminate simultaneously.
According to the older interpretation, *prajñā* is unable to illuminate all phenomena.
Upāya cannot illuminate the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa);
although they are observed together,
their functions of wisdom remain distinct.
This refers to the noble mind’s framework of being sealed by and adhering to two views.
A question was raised earlier: "Does *prajñā* not abide in skillful means while not realizing emptiness?"
Question: Why does it later state that "Upāya engages with existence without attachment, while Prajñā reflects emptiness without obstruction"?
Answer: There are two meanings to "non-attachment to emptiness."
First, prajñā illuminates the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Since the true mark has nothing upon which to rely,
prajñā likewise has nothing to which it clings.
This is the power of prajñā.
Second, not realizing emptiness is called non-attachment;
this is the power of upāya.
Not being attached to existence also possesses two meanings:
first, because *prajñā* enters into emptiness, one does not become attached to existence;
second, because skillful means (*upāya*) is guided by *prajñā*.
Therefore, one is able to traverse existence without being attached;
this, too, is the power of prajñā.
For this reason, it is further stated in the sūtra:
Prajñā does not cling to emptiness;
upāya does not cling to existence.
Or it is said:
Prajñā does not cling to existence;
upāya does not realize emptiness.
Each cites one aspect of the teaching, yet their meanings do not contradict one another.
Question: If prajñā illuminates emptiness and upāya reflects existence, then both wisdoms illuminate;
why, then, is it said that prajñā is without cognition?
Answer: Although prajñā does know, [it knows by way of non-cognition].
Yet there is nothing known;
although there is nothing known,
there is nothing not known.
Question: Since prajñā knows the true nature (dharmatā), it is said that there is "no-knowledge";
yet, since one also knows prajñā itself, it is likewise said that there is "no-knowledge.
Answer: Since two types of wisdom are distinguished based on these two objects, [the distinction is made].
Because Prajñā knows the true nature of reality (dharmatā), it is said to be "without knowledge.
One must not say that because one knows Prajñā, there is no knowledge.
If one were to know Prajñā [as an object], that would be skillful means (upāya).
Question: If Prajñā accords with the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), such that both internal and external are merged in obscurity and both object and contemplation are quiescent,
then while skillful means (upāya) illumines the conventional,
how can one know this Prajñā?
Answer: Prajñā is knowing through non-knowing as the means for that which is known;
it is non-knowing within knowing, which is precisely not-knowing as the means.
Question: Prajñā is "knowing through non-knowing" and "non-knowing while knowing.
Is it also possible for skillful means (upāya) to be so?
Answer: To point to the real as the provisional,
and to point to the provisional as the real—
the non-duality of the provisional and the real may also be understood in this way.
Where there is non-duality yet duality,
one knows through non-knowing;
this is called skillful means.
To know while being without knowing is called *prajñā*.
Question: Does *prajñā* illuminate emptiness by possessing both knowing and non-knowing?
What is so incorrect about using skillful means to discern this?
The answer is: while they are two, they are non-dual; both possess duality.
They are non-dual, yet dual.
The object known by Prajñā is emptiness,
while the wisdom that is able to know it exists;
therefore, it possesses both knowing and non-knowing.
However, because the skillful means (upāya) are capable of knowing, both the object of knowledge and the wisdom [that knows it] exist.
Thus, while [ordinary] consciousness may possess either knowledge or non-knowledge,
skillful means possesses only knowledge.
Question: How is it that Prajñā possesses knowledge while being without knowledge?
Answer: Prajñā knows the true nature of reality (dharmatā), wherein both the object of cognition and the observing subject are simultaneously quiescent;
therefore, it is without knowledge.
Yet, object and cognition remain distinct;
thus, knowing is not lost.
This is knowing through non-knowing.
To know is to be without knowing.
Question: If this is so, how does it differ from the "ultimate preservation" (*michun*) maintained by the Kaishan school?
Answer: As for their doctrine of ultimate preservation:
It ultimately does not reach the state of ultimate forgetting;
the meaning of ultimate forgetting never remains fully present.
Now, to exist extensively is considered ultimate non-existence;
because ultimate non-existence is itself extensive existence, they are distinct.
This is also true regarding the meaning of the "old" [tradition].
How is this different from the present?
Answer: When that [cognition] reaches the state of oblivion, consciousness ultimately does not function as an object, and the object ultimately does not constitute consciousness.
Thus, regarding these two views of object and cognition:
if cognition were identical to the object, then since the object lacks awareness,
cognition would likewise be devoid of knowing.
Cognition should also be thus.
If the object is cognition itself,
then since it is already present within cognition, it is inherently illuminated.
The same should apply to objects as well.
Now, in response to this single gate,
I shall briefly set forth the profound treasury of contemplative practice, the essential pivot of the Mahāyāna.
The Sūtra says:
"Lust is itself the Way;
so too are anger and delusion."
Within these three dharmas,
there are the paths of immeasurable Buddhas;
that which is desire is itself the path.
However, greed and desire are originally quiescent and pure by nature;
this is itself the true mark (dharmatā).
To realize this in such a manner is what is called prajñā.
How could the realm of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) be different from the contemplation of prajñā?
Therefore, object and wisdom are non-dual.
Although desire is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished, it nevertheless appears vividly as desire to sentient beings.
This is then called skillful means (upāya).
It is because one laments that what is not greed is called greed,
and thus desires to extract [the being] from it.
This skillful means is precisely what is called great compassion;
it seeks to cause [beings] to realize that desire is non-desire,
and to grant them the bliss of non-desire.
This very great compassion is also termed "loving-kindness.
Therefore, a single phrase of contemplative practice encompasses both the gateways of object and wisdom, as well as the two contemplations of loving-kindness and compassion.
Initially believing this Dharma is called the Ten Faiths;
next, understanding this Dharma is termed the Ten Understandings;
and finally, attaining realization and reaching ultimate penetration is termed the Buddha-mind.
Is it not the case that within a single contemplation of desire, one possesses the path of all Buddhas?
Next, we discuss two sutras.
Question: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is neither born nor extinguished, yet it can give rise to prajñā.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the twelve links of dependent origination are neither arising nor ceasing, which is brought forth by contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
Since both sūtras explain the relationship between the object and wisdom in this same way,
what difference is there between them?
The answer briefly clarifies four propositions:
first, the separation of cause and effect, and the separation of object and cognition;
second, the unification of cause and effect, and the unification of object and cognition.
Third, separating cause and effect while combining object and wisdom;
fourth, separating object and wisdom while combining cause and effect.
Regarding "separating cause and effect while separating object and wisdom":
Thus, that which is elucidated by Prajñā consists of the causal wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the aspects of the path,
while the result is all-knowledge and the knowledge of all modes.
This means opening up cause and effect.
Since true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) can give rise to *prajñā*,
it is the objective realm of true wisdom.
The conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) can give rise to skillful means (upāya);
it serves as the object of provisional wisdom (prajñā).
This refers to the opening up of both objects and wisdom.
Next, regarding the integration of cause and effect and the integration of object and wisdom,
it is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* concerning the meaning of the five natures (*pañca-gotra*).
First is the causal nature (*hetu-gotra*).
Second, the nature of the cause of causes;
third, the nature of the fruit;
fourth, the nature of the fruit of the fruit.
The five [factors] are neither cause nor effect in nature.
These five natures do not possess two distinct entities.
The sense of being able to produce the twelve links of dependent origination is termed "object" (*viṣaya*);
the sense of being produced [thereby] is termed... [result].
This is termed the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
Because this wisdom of contemplation is clear and lucid, it is called *bodhi*.
That *bodhi* is free from all burdens is itself the fruit of fruits (*phala-phala*).
However, the twelve links of dependent origination are pure by nature;
they have never possessed the relationship of cause and effect.
Furthermore, because it is neither object nor cognition, it is called "neither cause nor fruit.
Nevertheless, since these five natures lack two distinct entities,
the object is thereby transformed into cognition.
Conversely, cause and effect are as such;
they have never been cause and effect.
Therefore, it is called the "conjunction of cause and effect" and the "conjunction of object and cognition.

Third, regarding the "conjunction of cause and effect while distinguishing between object and cognition," this is also as stated in the *Pañcavimśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, where *prajñā* is taken as the cause and *sarvajñatā* as the effect.
Cause and effect do not possess two separate entities,
because the cause of prajñā is transformed into the fruit of sarvajña.
Master Kumārajīva said:
"Sarvajñā" (all-knowledge) is the elder Prajñā;
this name unifies cause and effect.
As for "opening up the object and the wisdom":
Although true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) can give rise to *prajñā*,
it does not transform the realm of true reality into *prajñā*,
nor does it transform the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
This is the wisdom of skillful means;
therefore, it is called the wisdom that opens up the objective realm.
Next is the wisdom that opens up the combined objective realm of cause and effect.
Furthermore, just as in *nirvāṇa*, because the object is transformed into wisdom,
it is called the "union of object and wisdom. Yet,
there exists a cause and its causal effect, as well as a cause and its resultant effect.
This explains cause and effect.
Question: Since the object is transformed into wisdom, and the cause is likewise transformed into the fruit, then the object and wisdom should both be conjoined in the same manner.
Answer: The Sūtra opens up the cause as the cause-cause and the effect as the effect-effect;
thus it is said that it "opens up cause and effect" while taking up object and cognition.
Since it simultaneously employs the designation "cause of causes" and eliminates the terminology of "object and cognition," it is said that object and cognition are conjoined.
Question: Why do these two sutras differ in their method of opening and closing [the exposition]?

Answer: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explains the meaning of object and wisdom by means of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), intending to clarify that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
Sentient beings are themselves the twelve links of dependent origination.
That which can produce through causes and conditions is the object;
that which is produced is wisdom.
Because there is no longer a dual nature, it clarifies the union of the object and the wisdom.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the true characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that gives rise to prajñā is explained;
that which is able to give rise [to it] is precisely unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) prajñā.
That which is produced is precisely conditioned observational wisdom;
therefore, one does not transform unconditioned prajñā,
because it constitutes conditioned prajñā.
This opens up the realm and wisdom.
All of these are non-dual yet dual;
therefore, the two sutras differ.
If two are non-dual, there is no further distinction.
This concludes the fifth section: The Gateway of Identity and Difference.
Question: Generally, there are five periods regarding the two wisdoms.
First, illuminating the phenomena within events is provisional (upāya);
discerning the principle of the Four Noble Truths is real (bhūta).
This refers to the two types of wisdom within the teachings of the Tripiṭaka:
the illumination of true emptiness is the ultimate (real),
while the discernment of conventional existence is the provisional (expedient).
This teaching of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* concerns two kinds of wisdom:
knowing the illness and identifying the medicine is the provisional (upāya);
administering the medicine according to the illness is the ultimate (bhūta).
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* speaks of two kinds of wisdom:
the four illuminations take the One Vehicle as the real,
while the discernment of the Two Vehicles as provisional.
The Lotus Sūtra speaks of two kinds of wisdom:
the fivefold illumination of the eternal is the real,
while the discernment of the impermanent is the provisional.
Nirvana consists of two kinds of wisdom.
What has been explained above is the interpretation of the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Question: Why do you say that the essential tenets of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* are misrepresented by the theory of five periods and the treatise on four schools? Answer:
These views deviate from the text and damage the meaning.
This has already been explained in detail previously;
now it shall be briefly stated.
Upon examining the contents of a single sutra:
It possesses five characters;
without depending on a beginning or an end,
it fully encompasses all wisdoms.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"The teachings of the three vehicles are explained in detail;
the bodhisattva universally studies all paths."
Thus, one recognizes that the principle of the Four Noble Truths is the ultimate,
while the phenomena within the realm of events are the provisional;
therefore, within the teachings of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there are the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and the two types of wisdom (*dvividha-jñāna*).
Prajñā reflects emptiness;
Upāya engages with existence.
These principles are extensively expounded throughout the ninety chapters of this sutra.
This refers to the two wisdoms of emptiness and existence;
the commentary, upon concluding the "Chapter on Certainty," cites the *Lotus Sūtra*.
This refers to the three, one, and two knowledges (*jñāna*).
The *Dharmasaṃgraha* states:
"The form bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas come and go."
The Dharma-body has no coming or going;
this is the twofold wisdom of the permanent and the impermanent.
It knows the illness and recognizes the medicine.
All the various sutras are complete;
there is no need to speak further of them.
Thus, regarding the single scripture, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
It is equipped with the two wisdoms of the five [aggregates].
In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, it is said that those who possess all forms of wisdom [are like this].
The "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter clarifies that self-discipline through the three emptinesses constitutes true wisdom,
while adorning the buddha-lands and transforming sentient beings constitute skillful means;
these are precisely the two wisdoms of emptiness and existence.
The "Chapter on Disciples" states:
"The Buddha-body is unconditioned;
it does not fall within the realm of numerical categories."
Furthermore, the appearance of the five turbidities of birth and death constitutes the two wisdoms of permanence and impermanence;
this is the Chapter on the Dharma Gate of Non-duality.
It clarifies that the mind of the śrāvaka and the mind of the bodhisattva are non-dual;
that is to say, the true wisdom of the One Vehicle illuminates the distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles, which is termed the provisional wisdom of the Three Vehicles.
Question: How is the gate of non-dual dharmas identical to the One Vehicle?
Answer: Because the principle of non-duality is the very foundation of the vehicle, it is called a "vehicle."
Because of the principle that their essence is non-dual,
one gives rise to the contemplation of non-duality;
by means of this contemplation of non-duality...
It can lead all practices to sarvajñā (omniscience). Therefore,
the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra* elucidates the profound meaning of the great divisions,
namely emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
By penetrating this meaning,
one penetrates the Mahāyāna and becomes fully endowed with the six pāramitās.
There is no obstruction.
Question: The principle of non-duality serves as the foundation for all three vehicles;
how can it be said that it is the foundation of the One Vehicle alone?
Answer: Since principle is fundamentally non-dual, how could there be three vehicles?
It is simply by uttering these words that one knows they all return to the One.
Furthermore, the principle of non-duality is another name for the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Moreover,
it further clarifies the eternal abiding [of the Buddha-nature].
Does this not clearly manifest the One Vehicle?
Therefore, we know that Vimalakīrti also possesses the five pairs of wisdoms.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, for those possessed of all wisdom,
the "Expedient Means" chapter states:
"Although I speak of nirvāṇa..."
This, too, is not true cessation.
All dharmas have, from the very beginning, been characterized by constant and inherent quiescence.
The nirvana of the past was not true cessation.
If the present nirvana is true cessation,
then the former nirvana was not truly eternal;
if the present nirvana is truly eternal, [the former was not].
Furthermore, in his commentary on the *Śāstra*, Vasubandhu fully elucidates the three bodies (*trikāya*) in the "Chapter on Lifespan. According to this,
the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) has both a beginning and an end.
The Reward Body has a beginning but no end;
the Dharma Body has neither beginning nor end.
Thus one should know.
It possesses the meaning of both permanence and impermanence.
Furthermore, if the fruit of the One Vehicle were still impermanent,
then its cause would differ from that of the Śrāvakas.
If the fruit were identical to the severance of ashes,
this would not be the case;
for the fruit of the śrāvaka is, in fact, the cause of the One Vehicle.
The "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" clarifies that knowing all phenomena as empty according to their true nature is genuine wisdom.
To know that which arises through causes and conditions is called the wisdom of skillful means;
it also encompasses both the wisdom of emptiness and the wisdom of existence.
The "Chapter on the Introduction" lists the assembly;
since it still praises the virtues of the śrāvakas according to the Hīnayāna,
we know this.
It also possesses the Three Piṭakas and the two types of knowledge;
that Nirvāṇa is complete with the five [qualities] goes without saying.
Question: If all forms of knowledge are contained within a single sūtra, [how is this so?]
What distinguishes these various sutras?
Answer: All Mahāyāna sutras generally serve to reveal the Path.
Since the Way is fundamentally non-dual,
how could its teachings possibly differ?
It is simply because there are many gateways for entry.
Regarding the distinctions between the various schools:
although a single sūtra may contain all five types,
the primary and secondary emphases of their explanations differ.
The Tripitaka and the One Vehicle teachings clarify only the phenomena and principle, and the provisional and the real;
they do not yet distinguish the other categories of the two wisdoms.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, emptiness and existence are treated as the primary meaning,
while other doctrines are secondary. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the threefold and singlefold [teachings] constitute the central principle.
The rest are all explained in a general manner.
Regarding nirvāṇa, permanence and impermanence are treated as primary;
the others are all elucidated concurrently.
Question: Why do the various sutras contain these distinctions between the lateral and the direct?
Answer: There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
those who proceed directly to the Buddha-way and [those who follow other paths].
Second, turning from the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle:
for bodhisattvas who proceed directly,
Prajñāpāramitā explains that through skillful means and true wisdom, one does not fall into the three realms.
Not abiding in the two vehicles,
there were two strong men,
each supporting one of his armpits.
Until one reaches the Buddha-way.
Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:
"There are sons of the Buddha."
"With a mind that is pure, gentle, and sharp of faculty—
I prophesy that such a person shall become a Buddha in a future age.
This refers to the time of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
It is unnecessary to clarify that the three vehicles are expedient means while the one vehicle is the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, for those who turn from the small toward the great,
their faculties have not yet been perfected at the time of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, rather than explicitly clarifying the meaning of the three vehicles as one,
the "Chapter on the Determination of the Lineage" cites the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to clarify those who regress and those who do not.
This is merely a secondary extension from the latter part of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding the three types of bhikṣus who cling to impermanence, by the time of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, [the teaching] reached its full development.
Because its roots have not yet been uprooted,
the eternal nature is not explained extensively;
since *prajñā* and *upāya* are both causal practices.
Furthermore, one must recognize the fruit and its virtues.
For this reason, the latter section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* briefly clarifies that while the Dharma-body is eternally traceless, it nonetheless manifests coming and going.
Moreover, this is because Sadāprarudita originally sought Prajñā.
Taking the two types of wisdom as correct,
because there is doubt regarding the Buddha’s coming and going within the Middle Way,
the text incidentally clarifies the fundamental and the manifested.
Question: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) prajñā and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) prajñā.
Does this not clearly distinguish between the permanent and the impermanent?
Answer: Unconditioned prajñā is of two kinds.
First, the objective realm of true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is called unconditioned prajñā;
the contemplative wisdom produced therefrom is called conditioned prajñā.
Second, the Dharma-body of the Buddha-fruit is called unconditioned prajñā.
The Bodhisattva’s wisdom based on causes is called conditioned *prajñā*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin jing) correctly clarifies that the object and the wisdom are the meaning of the unconditioned.
This explains that cause and effect are both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, the treatise says:
"If one wishes to attain conditioned Prajñā..."
"One should study non-conditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) prajñā.
This clarifies that if one wishes to attain contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), one must study the sphere of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
If it were said that one should study the fruit in order to attain the cause, [it would be incorrect].
This is not convenient in terms of meaning.
Furthermore, it is said that the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) can give rise to *prajñā*.
It is precisely through the object that wisdom arises.
If one were to say that the cause is produced by the fruit,
this interpretation would also be untenable.
If, according to the true mark (dharmatā), this Dharma-body takes suchness as the Buddha,
then this object and wisdom constitute cause and effect.
Within the aforementioned five phrases:
To clarify this point:
why is it that in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dapin) it is correct to define the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in terms of object and wisdom,
whereas in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* it is correct to define the unconditioned in terms of cause and fruit?
Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clearly explains that the practice of a bodhisattva is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) which can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because of wisdom, there is skillful means (*upāya*).
Therefore, the object and wisdom are taken as the primary [factors],
because Nirvana is the preeminent fruit of enlightened virtue;
all stages prior to that of the cause are impermanent.
The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is, from the outset, eternally abiding;
therefore, taking cause and effect as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the primary teaching.
Question: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that both object and wisdom are unconditioned.
What is meant by "the lateral and the direct"?
Answer: Although the realm of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the fundamental basis of *prajñā*, the Commentary (*Śāstra*) opens up *prajñā* into two types of wisdom.
The two types of wisdom are what give rise to it;
this is conditioned *prajñā*.
Therefore, that which is conditioned is correct.
Since the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is merely the objective sphere (ālambana), one cannot take that sphere as the thesis (pakṣa).

Question: In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is stated that by not dwelling in any phenomena, one dwells in *prajñā* and fulfills the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the myriad practices (*sādhana*).
"Is this conditioned or is it unconditioned?
He replied, "One who abides in non-abiding does not abide in any dharma that can be apprehended."
Because one does not dwell in any phenomena,
one dwells in prajñā;
this is the prajñā of the unconditioned true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Next, within the detailed exposition of the six pāramitās,
the sixth, prajñā, is the conditioned (saṃskṛta) prajñā.
This generally clarifies the sequence of the three dharmas.
The first is that which gives rise [to wisdom],
namely, the unconditioned *prajñā* of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
The second is the conditioned *prajñā* of the contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) that is produced.
The three guides accomplish the practice of cause and effect.
Question: How is it known that the non-abiding dharma is the abiding in *prajñā*, and that this is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of *prajñā*?
Answer: Since it is already conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) within the sixth perfection, it is thereby known.
The first is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, the treatise distinguishes the interpretations of the six schools regarding *prajñā*;
the sixth is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, because one abides in prajñā by means of the non-abiding dharma,
we know that the sixth [consciousness] is the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
The Lotus Sūtra is specifically intended for those who turn from the Lesser Vehicle to enter the Great Vehicle;
it clarifies that the three vehicles are merely expedient means.
It causes them to abandon the Lesser Vehicle,
demonstrates the One Vehicle as the ultimate reality,
and exhorts them to embrace the Great Vehicle.
This clearly elucidates the three [wisdoms] and the one [wisdom], which is prajñā.
Having abandoned the small for the sake of seeking the great,
one then gives rise to the bodhicitta.
In practicing the bodhisattva path,
one must study emptiness and existence, the provisional and the ultimate,
and remain unattached to the three realms.
One does not fall into the two vehicles but proceeds directly to the path of the Buddha; however,
since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* already explains this extensively, [this is not repeated here].
The Lotus Sūtra merely provides a brief exposition for the three types of śrāvakas at the assembly of the Lotus.
Because they do not cling to impermanence,
they have not yet clearly understood permanence and bliss;
however, since the cause of the One Vehicle has already been explained.
One must distinguish the fruit of the One Vehicle;
therefore, the final section briefly clarifies permanence.
Furthermore, it states that the doctrine of permanence establishes the preceding One Vehicle.
If it were impermanent,
it would again be identical to annihilation like ashes;
thus, it differs from the previous three [views].
Thus one knows that it is eternally abiding.
For this reason, I have briefly distinguished between the permanent and the impermanent.
Now the teaching of Nirvāṇa arises.
This is precisely because there is an attachment to impermanence;
therefore, the eternal is revealed.
As for the three—the empty, the existent, and the prior teaching—these have already been clarified.
I shall merely explain it briefly.

It is asked: if the *Prajñāpāramitā* is for bodhisattvas who proceed directly, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is for those of the Small Vehicle who turn back to enter the Great, then the conditions [for all beings] are already fully encompassed.
Question: For what purpose was the teaching of *nirvāṇa* established?
Answer: The establishment of the teaching has many intentions;
it cannot be understood through a single path alone.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites nineteen causes and conditions;
the purposes for which the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* was taught are not limited to one.
To explain this meaning according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
There are two kinds of sons:
the first are those who have lost their minds,
namely persons of dull faculties.
Second, those who do not lose their minds;
that is, those of sharp faculties.
Although there are both those who proceed directly and those who turn back, upon hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Lotus Sūtra*, they all attain awakening accordingly.
This refers to those with sharp faculties who have not lost their minds;
others with dull faculties who have lost their minds are still as yet unmedicated.
Only when he proclaimed his passing at the Twin Trees and preached the Nirvāṇa did people finally come to believe him. If this is so, then...
From the Lotus Treasury World up to the Vārāṇasī River, there are only two conditions:
those of sharp and dull faculties.
Prior to that point, it was for those of sharp faculties.
The teaching of Nirvana is for those of dull faculties;
furthermore, those who sit at the assemblies of Prajñā and the Lotus Sutra have all already attained the Way.
Now, having heard of nirvana,
one further advances toward awakening;
hence it is said:
For the sake of the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, who is like an elephant-king among men,
this sutra was preached.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for this.
First, they attain awakening after having traversed the teachings;
second, they immediately gain faith upon merely hearing of *Nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, [the teachings of] the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*...
Although there are two individuals,
[the Buddha] further explains the two wisdoms of nirvāṇa and separately discusses the two sūtras.
Question: What is the difference between the two types of wisdom in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*?
Answer: There are generally three explanations.
First, those who speak of the five periods of the teaching say: [text continues]
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* distinguishes two types of wisdom that illuminate emptiness and existence;
the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* involves knowing the illness and identifying the medicine to bestow instruction in accordance with conditions.
This has been explained above.
Regarding the doctrine of the four periods,
it is said that both the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* are subsumed within the second period.
Illuminating emptiness is the ultimate;
discerning existence is the provisional.
However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) explains both the shallow and the profound.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* specifically elucidates the teachings of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
People of the northern regions say that the *Vimalakīrti* is a teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuanton*).
"It is neither defiled nor pure, yet it moves through both defilement and purity.
Now, I say:
this is not so in either case.
The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas;
Expedient Means is their father.
They are the teachers of all beings.
There is nothing that does not arise from this.
This constitutes the two wisdoms of emptiness and existence;
it thus universally penetrates the Vaipulya teachings.
How could it be restricted to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* alone?
Furthermore, Prajñā (wisdom) mirrors emptiness while Upāya (expedient means) engages with existence;
this [pair] comprehensively subsumes all forms of knowledge.
Knowing the illness and identifying the medicine, one administers the medicine according to the illness;
the profound essence lies therein.
How could it be that the two wisdoms of *prajñā* do not encompass the provisional and the real of Vimalakīrti?
Therefore, [the previous] interpretation is incorrect.
Nāgārjuna expounded the ten great sūtras,
namely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and others.
Yet, Prajñāpāramitā is supreme.
How could one say that while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) explains both the shallow and the profound, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* alone clarifies the wondrous Way?
If it is argued that the Dharma in the *Vimalakīrti* is subtle because its interlocutor is a person of the eighth stage or above:
The Tathāgata taught Prajñāpāramitā as the ultimate fruit and virtue;
it must therefore be the most profound.
Furthermore, there were those such as Śāriputra and Subhūti, who were but ordinary persons.
To speak thus would not be the Great Dharma.
If it is claimed that the *Vimalakīrti* is profound because it demonstrates how the inconceivable can contain both the vast and the minute,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clearly points out that the power of a single hair can lift up a great trichiliocosm against the force of the wind.
Is this not clear?
Furthermore, Prajñāpāramitā and Upāya are the essence of the inconceivable;
borrowing a seat and requesting a meal are the manifestations of the inconceivable.
Just as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* sūtras distinguish the basis of the inconceivable through two types of wisdom,
so too does the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* manifest supernatural powers.
This reveals inconceivable traces.
How can it be that while the fundamental [teaching] is common to both the shallow and the deep, the traces alone are considered subtle?
If you argue that the three vehicles are common to both the shallow and the deep because they all study Prajñāpāramitā, [the response follows].
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* also clarifies that those of the two vehicles all take non-attainment as attainment;
how could this not be understood?
If one says that this sutra belongs to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (yuantun jiao), [how can it be reconciled with the aforementioned?]
This is also not the case.

Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other texts distinguish the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya*) and provisional paths as being diverse according to the specific needs of those to be transformed,
how can this sūtra alone be considered exclusively perfect and sudden (*yuan-dun*)?
What is clarified here is that the two types of wisdom elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* share both similarities and differences.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of Bodhisattvas, and skillful means (*upāya*) is their father; these two sūtras alike elucidate this Dharma.
However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (the *Dapin*) first clarifies true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).
The subsequent section distinguishes the skillful means;
thus, the ninety-chapter *Sūtra* is divided into two paths:
sixty-six chapters clarify Prajñā.
The subsequent twenty-four chapters clarify the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*).
As for why the true wisdom (*bhūta-prajñā*) was clarified first and the skillful means are now distinguished:
The true mark is the root;
all phenomena are the branches.
Because Prajñā illuminates the true mark.
Prajñā is the root,
for it illuminates all dharmas through skillful means;
skillful means is the branch.
This demonstrates the two roots and two branches;
from the root to the branch, it proceeds from essence to function.
Therefore, the preceding section clarifies actual wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*).
The subsequent section explains the skillful means.
Second, all views are of two kinds:
first, the view of existence; second, the view of non-existence.
Prajñā refutes the view of existence;
upāya destroys the view of non-existence,
thereby manifesting the Middle Way.
Because it remains far removed from the two extremes,
the former clarifies true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*),
while the latter distinguishes skillful means (*upāya*).
This refers to the sequence for refuting [wrong] views.
Third, there are two matters by which a bodhisattva regresses:
first, craving for the three realms; second, taking up the Lesser Vehicle.
Because of skillful means and true wisdom,
one does not cling to the three realms;
because of true wisdom and skillful means, [one does not cling].
They do not fall into the two vehicles;
they immediately enter the stage of a bodhisattva and attain the path of Buddhahood.
One must first transcend the three realms and subsequently transcend the two vehicles; therefore,
the true wisdom is explained first.
The following clarifies the skillful means.
This corresponds to the perilous and evil road of five hundred yojanas in the Lotus Sūtra;
the three realms constitute three hundred [yojanas].
The two vehicles constitute two hundred;
first they abandon three hundred,
and subsequently they abandon two hundred.
Therefore, the wisdom of reality is clarified first,
and the wisdom of skillful means is distinguished afterward;
thus, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin):
By combining the two vehicles, they total one hundred;
thus, only four hundred are clarified.
Although there are differences in whether they are expanded or condensed, [the number remains the same].
It is largely identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
as explained extensively therein.
Furthermore, Master Rui’s preface to the commentary states:
Because he correctly awakens to the spontaneous arising of perverse thoughts,
he composed the Āgamas;
because he clearly discerned that stagnation in existence arises from delusion, he composed them.
Prajñā illuminates this.
If it is so, then Prajñā is precisely that which shatters the "existence" of the Hīnayāna.
The preceding section clarified true wisdom;
although it destroys attachment to existence,
there remains the fear that one might instead realize emptiness.
The provisional means (upāya) refute emptiness;
this constitutes the sequence according to the progression of the teachings.
Fifth, the sequence as clarified by way of the stages (avasthā):
The preceding section elucidated the path of *prajñā*,
referring to the stages from the sixth ground downward;
next, it concerns the path of skillful means (*upāya*).
Thus, from the seventh stage upward, there is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
These are all stated as a general classification.
Nāgārjuna said:
Within Prajñā there is not an absence of upāya;
within upāya there is not an absence of Prajñā.
However, the former primarily elucidates Prajñā.
Later, the *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra* primarily elucidates skillful means (*upāya*).
Next, regarding the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which distinguishes between the two types of wisdom:
the former elucidates skillful means.
The subsequent discussion concerns reality.
The reason for this is that the emergence of this teaching was precisely occasioned by illness.
Therefore it is said:
"He manifested illness through skillful means;
because of this illness, there were two assemblies at Fangzhang and An Yuan."
Therefore, the former clarifies the skillful means,
while the latter distinguishes the reality.
Furthermore, it concerns the maturing of sentient beings and the purification of Buddha-lands.
This is because it is the application of the bodhisattva’s skillful means.
The chapter on the Buddha-land clarifies the pure buddha-field.
Having already departed through skillful means,
he brings sentient beings to fulfillment;
therefore, this sutra extensively elucidates skillful means.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Dapin*) predominantly elucidates the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*),
while manifesting few supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* (*Jingming*) predominantly manifests supernatural powers.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* primarily elucidates the true aspect (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* largely elucidates true wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*),
while the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* extensively distinguishes between the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real.
Question: What is the difference between *upāya* (expedient means) and *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means)?
Answer: In their general sense, there is no distinction;
both carry the meaning of being skillful.
Speaking of them separately,
expedient means (*upāya*) is long,
while provisional speech (*prajñapti-vāk*) is short.
Now, the three phrases are explained in general:
first, illuminating the true nature (dharmatā) is real wisdom;
discerning the myriad phenomena is expedient means.
Second, quiescent discernment regards the myriad phenomena as the Real;
externally reversing movement is taken as the Expedient.
Third, it accords with dynamic function.
To take this non-ailing body as real and to feign illness within the quarters as provisional:
the initial illumination of the true mark (dharmatā) is called real wisdom (bhūta-prajñā).
As for the remaining three gates,
they all belong to the category of skillful means; therefore,
their provisional meaning is limited.
However, taking only the outward manifestation of contrariety and naming it "expedient means" (upāya),
expedient means is thus a specific function within the category of skillful methods;
this is why it is described as "short."
Question: Since there are differences in length between provisional means (*upāya*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), is it likewise the case for the two truths?
Answer: The truth of skillful means is long.
In terms of provisional and ultimate truth,
it is brief. The reason for this is that skillful means (upāya) is capable of accomplishing everything.
True wisdom illuminates that which there is nothing it does not accomplish, yet in reality there is nothing accomplished;
therefore, it is eternal.
Expedient wisdom merely involves movement within the realm of existence.
True wisdom is the tranquil discernment within existence;
therefore, when contrasted with the provisional, it is "short.
Question: Does the outward manifestation of contrived movement constitute the provisional?
Thus, illumination is such that movement is non-movement; this is the real.
But do these two [distinctions] merely establish the provisional and the real?
Answer: Externally manifesting the reversal of movement is the provisional.
This is administering medicine according to the illness;
one must internally remain tranquil and examine the faculties to ensure the medicine is authentic,
only then will the two types of wisdom be perfected.
Because the wisdom of emptiness does not know the medicinal roots, the two types of wisdom are not accomplished.
This concludes the sixth section: The Gate of Length and Shortness.
A general discussion of the various sutras contains four propositions.
First: true wisdom is long and expedient wisdom is short.
Second, the provisional is long and the real is short;
third, both are long;
fourth, both are short.
Regarding the statement that "true wisdom is long and expedient wisdom is short":
this distinguishes the two types of wisdom based on movement and stillness.
Stillness, which discerns both emptiness and existence, is considered true wisdom.
Ultimate reality is indeed the long-term;
external, responsive movement constitutes the provisional.
The provisional is merely that which is functionally effective.
This is why it is considered "short.

Question: Since the internal stillness that discerns emptiness and existence possesses real wisdom, which is already "long," why does the external movement speak dualistically of both emptiness and existence?
As it is said regarding the two truths,
emptiness and existence are manifested together;
for example, when Mañjuśrī manifested a body of empty space for King Śibi.
Furthermore, he manifests a body sixteen feet tall or eight thousand feet tall.
If such movement and function thus penetrate both emptiness and existence,
then both wisdoms are fully developed.
Answer: Although it is said externally that there is emptiness and existence,
because the wisdom that discerns existence arises [from within],
it is provisionally considered short.
Regarding the statement that "the provisional is long and the real is short," this refers to taking the discernment of emptiness as the real and the illumination of existence as the provisional.
Within the division of the two wisdoms, the illumination of emptiness is the real.
True wisdom is called "short" because it consists solely of quiescent discernment;
it illuminates the provisional [wisdom] of the conditioned.
The provisional is complete in both movement and stillness; internally illuminating the roots and medicines constitutes its aspect of stillness.
Bestowing medicine in response to external illnesses constitutes movement;
because provisional means (upāya) penetrate both movement and stillness, it is said to be "long.
As for the two wisdoms being both long:
One distinguishes between the provisional and the real based on emptiness and existence:
real wisdom illuminates emptiness,
while provisional wisdom discerns existence.
Within the midst of existence, one clearly perceives the two modes of existence: motion and stillness.
Through true wisdom, one illumines emptiness, such that both motion and stillness are seen as empty.
Therefore, these two knowledges have neither superiority nor inferiority.
As for both knowledges being equally short,
they are merely distinguished as two within the context of their application.
Internally, they are quiescently reflective of the reality of conditioned phenomena;
externally, they are dynamically active as skillful means.
Therefore, both are deficient.
It is also like the case where Vimalakīrti’s lack of illness is the reality, while his manifesting of sickness is the provisional;
the question is that while the distinction between the provisional and the real is established based on wisdom regarding existence,
it may likewise be established based on the wisdom that illuminates emptiness.
Answer: True wisdom clarifies the meaning of both duality and non-duality;
furthermore, it accords with their essential nature, and for this reason, they are not differentiated.
Skillful means and wisdom are the non-dual meaning of duality;
furthermore, they function as its application,
thereby opening up the two.

If one wishes to categorize them: illuminating the shallowness of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is provisional, while discerning the depth of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is real.
Furthermore, the emptiness of the two vehicles is termed provisional emptiness.
The emptiness of a bodhisattva is called "actual emptiness.
Based on these two aspects of emptiness—the provisional and the actual—one may also establish the two types of wisdom: provisional wisdom and actual wisdom.
The Seventh Section on the Six Wisdoms.
Formerly, the Venerable Master of Xinghuang Monastery lectured on this sutra.
This clarifies the six kinds of twofold wisdom,
which are organized into three pairs:
namely, the provisional and the real, and skillful means and the real.
There are the real skillful means (*upāya*) and the provisional skillful means; there are also the skillful means that are both provisional and real.
Therefore, there are two realities, two provisos, and two types of skillful means.
Regarding "the reality of skillful means" (*upāya-tattva*):
it is distinguished as "reality" in contrast to "skillful means.
It is called "reality" because it refers to the wisdom that knows the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the provisional and the ultimate,
there are generally two senses.
First, they are distinguished from the perspective of the bodhisattva.
Just as the provisional is used to illuminate the conditioned,
within this very provisional,
the real is further elucidated.
Just as internal stillness and discernment, with the medicinal roots as the reality,
while external movement is the provisional, it is therefore called "provisional and real.
Furthermore, just as a body free from illness is the reality within the provisional.
This also clarifies the provisional and the real.
Second, regarding the clarification of the provisional and the real in relation to the śrāvakas:
the wisdom of the two vehicles that illuminates phenomena is the provisional.
To discern the principle of suffering and emptiness as the reality,
and now to clarify the reality of the Two Vehicles by contrasting the great aspiration with the small understanding,
is essentially to manifest the provisional in order to reveal the real.
It is not the ultimate reality.
Next, it is said in pairs:
"the real skillful means" and "the provisional skillful means."
Real skillful means:
the wisdom that directly confronts the true nature of reality (dharmatā) is called real skillful means.
As for provisional skillful means:
This clarifies that, in contrast to the reality of the two vehicles mentioned above, these two vehicles are merely provisional expedients (*upāya*).
Thus it is said: "The three pairs."
Regarding "the provisional based on the real" (shiquan fangbian quan):
the provisional based on the real refers to arising the provisional from the real;
therefore, it is called "the provisional based on the real."
Just as both emptiness and existence are called "real" when illuminated, yet they are designated as "expedient" based solely on their external function;
furthermore, regarding "the real and the expedient," the expedient of the two vehicles is a false expedient.
The expedient means of a bodhisattva is called "true expedient means.
Regarding these expedient means,
taking the illumination of emptiness as the truth is what constitutes their reality.
Illuminating the skillful means regarding conditioned phenomena,
within those very skillful means,
one further gives rise to provisional expedients.
Thus, internal illumination of the reality of the conditioned is the ultimate, while external dynamic application is the provisional;
these six gates establish the meaning of long and short.
This concludes the eighth section, the Gate of Opening and Closing.
The two types of wisdom possess four permutations regarding their opening and closing.
First, the opening of the two kinds of prajñā is as previously explained.
Because it illuminates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, it is called *prajñā*.
Because it illuminates all phenomena as they truly are, it is called *upāya*.
Since the Tathāgata internally illuminates these two, he possesses these two types of wisdom.
Because the Buddha is born from these two,
he has a father and a mother;
for the sake of sentient beings, he further explains these two.
As the *Śāstra* states:
first, the path of prajñā is taught;
next, the path of upāya is elucidated.
First, the sutras of the Buddha-mother are elucidated;
next, the sutras of the Buddha-father are elucidated.
Therefore, Prajñā is the honored sutra that serves as the father and mother to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
To believe in it brings great merit;
to disparage it invites great transgression.
Since you have already stated that the two types of wisdom are its parents:
What are the "grandparents"?
Answer: When distinguished by way of object and wisdom, they are the two objects:
the true aspect (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and all phenomena (dharmas).
It is able to give rise to two kinds of wisdom;
these are the paternal and maternal grandfathers.
Therefore, *er yan* (the two conditions) are called the "mothers of wisdom."
If we discuss this based on the sequence of practice,
it is through great compassion that prajñā arises;
thus, great compassion is the mother of prajñā.
Furthermore, it is because of great compassion that there is skillful means;
this [compassion] is the mother of skillful means,
which carries the same meaning as "father."
It is simply that they are spoken of in combination.
This is precisely the opening up of the two types of wisdom.
Question: If Prajñā is taken as the mother and Upāya as the father, [what is the result?]
Why does the treatise state that Prajñā is the mother and the Pratyutpanna Samādhi is the father?
Furthermore, why does it say that Prajñā is the mother and the five perfections are the father?
Answer: *Pratyutpanna* is translated as "manifest before one's eyes."
"Manifesting" means seeing the Buddha face-to-face;
this constitutes "with effort."
Therefore, they are categorized under skillful means and designated as the "father.
The practice of the five perfections is likewise categorized under skillful means.
Next, regarding the second synthesis of the two wisdoms:
it clarifies that both *prajñā* (wisdom) and *upāya* (skillful means) are *prajñā*.
The reason for this is as follows:
Prajñā is the essence and upāya is the function.
The essence is the essence of prajñā;
the function is the function of prajñā.
Therefore, all are named Prajñā.
Although the Tathāgata has expounded the ninety chapters of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*,
both [the large and small versions] are referred to as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* within the two paths.
Since the latter is not employed as a means [to the former],
we know that both types of wisdom are called *prajñā*. Furthermore, as the treatise says:
Just as various objects fashioned from gold are nothing other than gold itself and possess no separate essence, so too,
within the six perfections, skillful means combined with true wisdom are both designated as *prajñā*.
Question: How is this known to be so?
Answer: The other five perfections merely clarify five kinds of practice.
One does not distinguish between the illumination of emptiness and the knowledge of existence.
Now, the meaning of illuminating emptiness belongs to Prajñā;
the meaning of knowing existence also belongs to Prajñā.
Thus we know that both types of wisdom are called *prajñā*;
this means that when expedient means (*upāya*) and reality (*tattva*) are combined, they are both designated by the term "reality" (*tattvārtha*).
Third, regarding the point that both the provisional and the real are termed "provisional":
since illumination of the state of effort (*sābhoga*) is already called a "skillful means" (*upāya*),
so too is the skillfulness of illuminating emptiness.
This is also because they are both skillful means.
The two illuminations are equally skillful;
that is, both are skillful means.
Furthermore, regarding that which is called the "perfection of skillful means" (upāya-pāramitā) in the seventh stage,
the Commentary states:
"At this time, because prajñā is pure, it is conversely named 'skillful means'."
Because the function of prajñā is not yet subtle up to the sixth bhūmi,
it is not called "skillful means" (upāya).
Upon reaching the seventh bhūmi, because the function of prajñā is subtle, it is called "skillful means."
As stated in the text of the Seventh Ground, from the wisdom of skillful means arise the ten sublime practices;
although one knows that the three realms are empty, one nonetheless adorns the three realms and so forth.
Therefore, it is known.
Both types of wisdom are termed "expedient means" (upāya).
In accordance with this principle,
it is also possible for both expedient means and prajñā in the sixth bhūmi to be designated as "prajñā."
Furthermore, as the Śrīmālā-sūtra says, the One Vehicle is a great skillful means.
Within this One Vehicle,
whether one illuminates emptiness or illuminates existence, [it is all encompassed].
To speak of emptiness and to speak of existence are both termed skillful means,
for they are all the great pedagogical artistry of the Buddhas.
This is also the unification of the two wisdoms as a skillful means.
Fourth is neither opening nor closing;
this is the sublation of the three preceding phrases to clarify all phenomena.
Right contemplation has never been real,
nor has it ever been provisional,
nor has it ever been revealed.
Furthermore, they have never been joined.
Therefore it is said: "This Dharma cannot be shown; its verbal expressions are quiescent.
The Buddha cannot practice it, nor can the Buddha reach it."
Now, those who possess the real power of opening and closing [the teachings] do so entirely for the sake of sentient beings emerging from within the realm of namelessness and signlessness.
This merely clarifies the differences in the modes of opening and closing [the gates].
This is the ninth section, the Gate of Severance and Subjugation.
First, it relies upon the *Madhyamaka-śāstra-vṛtti*.
First, the doctrines of other schools are established, and then they are examined.
A question is asked: how do the two types of knowledge sever the afflictions?
The answer is that this sutra states:
"The Buddha taught the severance of afflictions for those with overweening pride;
in reality, there is no severance."
Question: All the major and minor sūtras and śāstras clarify the severing of delusions.
Why, then, do you say they are not severed?
Answer: If you say they are abandoned, I now ask you this:
is there any delusion that can be abandoned?
If something exists in reality, it cannot be severed.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"If a phenomenon existed previously and later ceases to exist..."
If the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas already possess faults and transgressions,
how can you say they have severed them? If,
on the other hand, they were free from delusion, [how could there be faults]?
Ultimately, what is it that is abandoned?
Furthermore, the presence of delusion is itself the view of existence;
the absence of delusion is termed the view of non-existence.
"Both 'existence' and 'non-existence,' as well as 'neither existence nor non-existence,' are all afflictions.
How can afflictions sever afflictions?"
Furthermore, even if there are afflictions to be abandoned, wisdom is that which abandons them.
Is it because of the delusions of view that they are abandoned, or are they abandoned without seeing?
If it were by means of seeing, then light and darkness would coexist.
How is it abandoned?
If they do not see one another,
what further could there be to abandon?
If one were to claim that understanding and delusion are mutually exclusive and thus categorically distinct,
then the single instance of understanding represented by the Indian Dīpaṃkara would simply destroy the darkness of China.
It eliminates all delusions.
Furthermore, while wisdom alone is capable of severing them,
it does so in conjunction with its auxiliary companions.
If wisdom alone were able to sever [the afflictions],
why would a bodhisattva cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path?
Wisdom alone does not effect severance.
Even with a companion,
they still cannot sever it;
just as one blind person cannot see, so it is with many blind people.
Furthermore, does the severance occur in a single moment, or as a continuous process?
If it occurs in a single moment, then the affliction would likewise be a single moment,
and both would vanish simultaneously.
How can it be severed?
If it is a continuity that is severed,
is it severed because the continuity has been extinguished, or is it severed while the continuity is not yet extinguished?
If it were extinguished, there would be nothing to continue;
if it were not extinguished, there could be no continuation.
How, then, does it continue?
Inferring from this,
there is nothing to be severed;
therefore, one should not say that wisdom severs delusions.
Question: If that were so, there would be no abandonment [of afflictions].
Why, then, does the Sūtra say that "the wisdom associated with a single thought-moment abandons the habitual tendencies of the afflictions"?
Answer: As deduced above, there is ultimately no severance.
To realize this is itself severance.
The reason for this is that when one seeks the origin of delusion or enlightenment in all places, they are found nowhere; thus,
the mind has nothing upon which to rely.
When the mind has no basis,
all burdens are purified; therefore,
it is called "severance."
There is no contradiction between severance and non-severance.
Question: Since that which is called "severance" is defined by having nothing upon which to rely, is it severed by *prajñā* (wisdom) or by *upāya* (skillful means)?
The answer is: It is traditionally said that because *prajñā* is the wisdom of emptiness, it severs [defilements];
whereas because skillful means (*upāya*) illuminates existence, it does not sever them.
Now it is clear that when there is something to be attained, both the wisdom of emptiness and the wisdom of existence are unable to sever [the afflictions];
when there is nothing to be attained, both emptiness and existence are able to sever them.
However, though non-dual, it appears as two.
This opens up two types of wisdom that differ from one another:
the wisdom of skillful means and the wisdom of reality.
This is to sever while not severing;
it is the skillful means of true wisdom.
It is to sever while not severing.
Question: Why is this so? Answer:
Because there is that upon which one relies and clings;
this is the root of all afflictions.
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is the foundation of non-attachment.
Because this true reality has no basis, it gives rise to *prajñā*.
Because Prajñā is characterized by non-attachment, the various delusions are purified;
therefore, it is called "severance.
Question: If wisdom arises in conjunction with its object, how is this so?
If that is so, how does this severance of delusions differ from that of others?
The answer is: it is not said that there is a real characteristic (dharmatā) existing separately outside of delusion; rather, one realizes the real characteristic and thereby severs them.
One simply understands that afflictions are fundamentally non-arising from the beginning and are likewise non-extinguishing now.
This is precisely the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa);
therefore, it is called "the severance that accords with the true mark.
Question: Is it only through prajñā that [afflictions] are severed, or does sarvajñā also sever them?
In response to this point, there were two ancient masters who held differing views:
one said that the severing of the adamantine mind is the severing by *prajñā*.
Some say that what is severed by the Buddha’s wisdom is severed by *sarvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom).
Now, this is clarified:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The bodhisattva proceeds within the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*);
the Buddha proceeds within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)."
There is no darkness whatsoever.
Examining the meaning of this passage,
there is the sense that both unimpeded liberation and its counterpart possess the qualities of being abandoned and not abandoned.
If, through a single moment of correct contemplation, delusions do not manifest before one,
this is unimpeded right severance;
one attains liberation and dwells beyond all entanglements.
Therefore, liberation is uninterrupted.
Thus it is said:
"The Buddha walks upon the path of liberation."
There is no darkness whatsoever.
If one says that liberation continues into a state of unimpededness where there is no delusion before one and which obstructs future delusions so that they cannot arise in succession,
then there would be an act of obstruction and severance.
Therefore, it is also called "abandonment," because it is the unimpeded right abandonment;
thus one may say that the vajra-like [samādhi] has exhausted all delusions.
Since liberation does not prevent the future afflictions from arising,
it cannot be said that they are exhausted;
for since both exhaustion and non-exhaustion are mutually non-contradictory, [there is no conflict].
Question: Is *prajñā* (wisdom) non-obstruction and *sarvajñā* (omniscience) liberation?
Can it be said that the stages prior to the [first] ground constitute non-obstruction and the first ground constitutes liberation? Answer: Some say:
The same applies here:
in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), because the practice prior to the patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti) has not yet been long cultivated,
it merely suppresses [the afflictions] but does not sever them.
"In the Mahāyāna, one practices prior to the [first] bhūmi for a long duration;
therefore, one is able to sever [the afflictions].
Now, I say this is not so."
The doctrines of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ vastly in their relative superiority; nevertheless,
the Tathāgata established them according to a grand, overarching framework that is fundamentally similar.
In the Hīnayāna, the seven stages of preparation (saptayogācāra) suppress [the afflictions], while the stage of patience (kṣānti) eliminates them.
In the Mahāyāna, the thirty minds (triṃśaccitta) suppress them, and they are eliminated at the first stage (prathamabhūmi).
Within the first stage, one spontaneously attains the unhindered liberations (anāvaraṇavimokṣa).
The unimpeded right abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa*) and liberation (*vimukti*) are as explained above.
Question: Is it that the unimpeded [state] is transformed into liberation?
Is it that liberation arises through the cessation of obstacles?
The answer is: according to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā), it is through cessation; according to the Saṃghabhadra-śāstra (Tattvasiddhi), it is through transformation.
The refutation of these two views has already been clarified elsewhere; here,
I shall briefly set them forth.
If the vajra were to perish and there were a separate fruit of Buddhahood,
why would *prajñā* be called *sarvajñā*?
How could one become a Buddha by transforming the vajra?
How can that which is subject to transformation and impermanence be made permanent? Herein,
it is clarified that there exists both transformation and non-transformation, as well as non-decay and non-non-decay.
